transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-06-01 16:00 UTC | Duration: 48 mins | Recording on
Attendees: Ava Martinez, Noah Chen (Redwood); Maya Thompson, Luis Ortega, Priya Rao, Benji (Sapphire Park)

Summary: quick discovery on reserved capacity vs ephemeral burst. Customer has a multi-tenant inference path for 2 product lines, needs isolation for PII-sensitive predictions, wants low-latency tail (95th < 150ms), but also unpredictable weekend spikes (10x). Exploring Dedicated reserved nodes + hot ephemeral burst.

[00:00] Ava: hey everyone thanks for joining, can you hear me ok?
[00:04] Maya: yeah loud and clear, thanks Ava.
[00:06] Priya: yup, good to go.
[00:10] Ava: quick intros — I'm Ava, AE on Redwood inference, and with me is Noah our SE. maybe go around?
[00:15] Maya: I'm Maya, CTO at Sapphire Park. we run two main products, DataSynth for synthetic data and RealTimeQA for support automation.
[00:22] Luis: Luis, platform eng, day-to-day infra and costs, we own k8s and some GCP projects.
[00:27] Priya: Priya, VP product, focused on uptime and user experience.
[00:30] Benji: Benji, SRE, I'll probably ask about failover and runbooks. (audio glitch)

[00:39] Ava: cool, goal for today is to understand your isolation needs, burst patterns, and what success looks like if you go Dedicated vs Hosted vs on-prem. we can surface tradeoffs on latency/cost and scaling.

[00:52] Priya: the immediate thing is compliance and PII isolation for RealTimeQA, some customers require their prompts never touch shared pools. so we need tenant-level isolation or VPC-private option.

[01:05] Noah: totally understood. we support Reserved Dedicated pools that can be single-tenant or fenced tenants with network isolation / VPC peering to your project. question — is it strict physical tenancy you need or logical isolation with encryption + audit?

[01:20] Maya: short answer: some contracts ask for strict tenancy but majority we can live with cryptographic isolation + audit for now. however if we sign enterprise deals we'll need the stronger path. so we want a hybrid plan — start with fenced dedicated and evaluate on-prem later.

[01:38] Ava: great. can you walk us through expected qps and request shape? average tokens? prompt lengths? and when do spikes happen?

[01:47] Luis: baseline RealTimeQA is about 70 qps across all regions, peaks go to 600 qps during US business hours for big customers, and then DataSynth does large batch generation once nightly — often long sequences 2k+ tokens for each job.

[02:05] Priya: weekend spikes are the tricky bit — marketing campaigns sometimes create 8-10x bursts for minutes to hours.

[02:14] Noah: got it. are the burst requests latency-sensitive (interactive) or can they be queued?

[02:19] Maya: interactive, must be low latency for RealTimeQA — 95th under 150ms ideally. DataSynth batch can tolerate higher latencies.

[02:28] Noah: ok that suggests we should split workloads — dedicated low-latency pool pinned to small models or quantized variants and a separate warm pool for DataSynth. Redwood supports warm prewarmed 'hot pools' and also ephemeral burst nodes — we can explain tradeoffs.

[02:44] Benji: quick question: in case a hot pool prewarm can't handle surge, is there automatic fallback to hosted multitenant? what about data residency then?

[02:55] Ava: yes we can configure fallback policies. fallback can route to a sanitized hosted variant but that would need contractual agreement for data residency/privacy; usually customers set fallback to a compatible on-prem or Dedicated overflow so data doesn't leave their region.

[03:13] Priya: we need to avoid sending PII to shared pools. fallback to hosted might be a no-go for RealTimeQA, ok for DataSynth though.

[03:22] Noah: noted. we can map policies per route. also you mentioned 2k+ token batch jobs — those are heavy on memory, we'll want node classes with larger GPU memory or model sharding. what's your model family, are you running open LLMs or managed models?

[03:36] Maya: open models currently, mix of Llama-3 style and some small finetuned models. we're exploring quantized 4-bit for cost reasons.

[03:44] Noah: good — runtime supports quantized kernels; quantization changes batching characteristics and latency. we'll include guidance on recommended kernels and batch sizes.

[03:53] Luis: curious on autoscaling — can dedicated reserved pools burst above reserved capacity for short periods? we saw Redwood mention burst capacity in docs.

[04:02] Ava: yes, reserved pools can be configured with burst capacity (contractual). there's also a warm-pool prewarm approach where you keep a small hot pool ready and spin ephemeral nodes. tradeoff is cost vs hard SLA.

[04:15] Maya: can you give an example cost profile? like if we reserve x nodes and then pay for bursts how does that look? rough numbers ok.

[04:23] Ava: rough example: reserving 4 A100-equivalent nodes might cover baseline; burst capacity (on-demand) is charged at higher unit rate. we typically show a blended number: reserve for 70-80% of predictable consumption, burst covers the rest. we'll send a sizing + pricing table.

[04:38] Priya: what's typical cold start from ephemeral? like spin-up time to be ready to accept tokens?

[04:43] Noah: depends on image + model size; prewarmed hot pool is immediate, ephemeral node boot and model load is network+IO bound, can be 30s to 3 minutes for large models. for interactive low-latency you want hot instances.

[04:57] Benji: what about KV cache warmups — can cache be shared across nodes or is it per node? we worry about repeated context causing tail spikes.

[05:06] Noah: KV cache is per replica; we do prefix caching and have warm cache strategies when routing requests to same model/tenant. but if you have stateless ephemeral nodes, first requests will be slower until cache warms. we can route sticky sessions to preserve cache affinity.

[05:22] Luis: sticky routing — that can increase unevenness though, how do you handle load balancing?

[05:27] Noah: policy-based routing: you can choose latency-first sticky routing for interactive endpoints and throughput-first for batch. Redwood console exposes these toggles, and you can do canary fallbacks if a node crosses SLO.

[05:40] Maya: on the security checklist — SOC2, KMS integration, SSO/SAML, audit logs — do you support customer-managed KMS?

[05:48] Ava: yes we support customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM) for private deployments and Dedicated with key encryption at rest. audit logs can be delivered to your SIEM. SSO via SAML/OIDC is supported. we'll attach the security pack.

[06:00] Priya: do you have any customers who require air-gapped on-prem eventually? what's the timeline for migrating a pilot to private deployment?

[06:08] Noah: we've done private installs; timeline varies but pilot to private can be 8-14 weeks depending on networking and approvals. we'll map a migration plan if you need it.

[06:19] Luis: ok. one last infra question: our k8s team prefers to keep all egress through a narrow set of IPs and use NAT. can Redwood's private control plane talk over fixed egress IPs?

[06:30] Ava: yes, for Dedicated we can provide peering + static egress ranges for customer-owned firewalls. for Private on-prem you control the network entirely.

[06:38] Maya: switching to SLAs — what's the expected 95th latency guarantee for dedicated small models vs large seq models?

[06:47] Noah: for interactive small models on pinned capacity we can aim for 95th < 150ms; for long sequences (2k) on heavy models 95th will be higher and we usually recommend a separate batch pipeline with higher latency tolerance. SLAs are contractable and depend on reserved node counts and redundancy.

[07:05] Priya: we will need multi-AZ redundancy for mission-critical endpoints — can dedicated pools span AZs?

[07:11] Ava: yes, pools can be configured across zones with failover policies, but that impacts prewarm behavior and KV locality — we'll document tradeoffs.

[07:23] Maya: curious about version pinning & rollouts. we can't afford regressions after deploys. how do you do canaries and automatic fallback?

[07:30] Noah: Redwood supports canary rollouts, traffic split, and automatic rollback if latency or quality regressions exceed thresholds. you can pin a tenant to a model version while letting others use newer versions. we also integrate evaluation prompts to detect quality regressions.

[07:46] Luis: how do you measure "quality"? we have strict business KPIs.

[07:50] Noah: you define eval suites (prompts + expected output scoring). Redwood Optimize can run continuous evals and alert on drift or regressions.

[07:58] Maya: ok. also licensing: if we use open models but want commercial redistribution, any constraints from Redwood?

[08:05] Ava: Redwood is model-agnostic; license compliance is on the customer. we can help capture model provenance and note known licenses.

[08:14] Priya: let's be practical — what's the minimal pilot that'll validate Dedicated for us?

[08:19] Ava: usually it's a 4-week pilot: reserve a small Dedicated pool, run a subset of traffic (10-20%) behind a feature flag, execute bench runs and measure 95/99 latency, throughput, and cost. then decide to scale/reserve.

[08:32] Maya: sounds reasonable. do you support usage-based bridging billing if pilot spikes? so we don't have to commit too many dollars upfront.

[08:40] Ava: yes we have pilot terms where we can provide temporary burst credits or a short-term overage rate for pilots. we'll propose terms in the pricing sheet.

[08:50] Benji: bench question: what exact metrics should we capture to compare to our current on-prem cluster?

[08:56] Noah: collect QPS, p50/p95/p99 latency, token/sec, GPU utilization, memory usage, cold-start times, and cost per 1M tokens. also capture input/output token histograms and distribution of sequence lengths.

[09:12] Luis: we'll share a 7-day histogram but need to anonymize some fields.

[09:16] Priya: can Redwood run the bench for us or do we run it from our side?

[09:20] Noah: our SEs can run bench with a shared test harness; best is joint run — we supply test prompts and scripts, you supply traffic traces or we replay synthetic traffic.

[09:30] Ava: switching to pricing nuances — quantization + batching reduces cost significantly but may affect latency. we can model different quant and batch combos.

[09:40] Maya: do you have examples of customers who did reserved + quantize and saved 30-50%?

[09:45] Ava: yes, we have case studies; we'll include an anonymized one showing ~40% reduction after quant and kernel tuning.

[09:52] Luis: about monitoring — can we get token-level cost breakdown and per-route dashboards?

[09:58] Noah: yes Redwood Console shows per-route/model/token breakdown, per-token cost, and tracing hooks to correlate latency to downstream services.

[10:07] Priya: any limitations on model size for warm pools? what if we want 70B+ models?

[10:12] Noah: larger models require more GPU memory; we support sharded execution for very large models and also recommend sequence slicing for batch. warm pools for huge models are costlier but possible; we'll show options.

[10:23] Maya: ok, let's talk SLA numbers and redundancy in more detail next session. for now, can you outline recommended node classes if we want 95th <150ms at peak 600 qps with 10-20% spike headroom?

[10:34] Noah: initial recommendation: 6 x A100-eq nodes (or 8 x A40-eq) pinned for interactive; plus a 2-node hot prewarm to handle burst for a few minutes; DataSynth batch on separate 2 large-memory nodes. exact numbers depend on batching and quant. we'll provide a sizing matrix.

[10:52] Priya: interesting — any limit on number of pinned tenants per node? we want to keep heavy customers isolated.

[10:58] Noah: you can create tenant pools or per-tenant reservations; pin heavy customers to isolated slices. licensing applies.

[11:06] Ava: I'll recap action items at the end but quick question: are there procurement constraints or timelines for signing reserved capacity?

[11:13] Priya: we typically have quarterly procurement cycles, but for strategic enterprise sales we can accelerate. target decision window Q3 if pilot looks good.

[11:22] Maya: also legal needs to see DPA and data flow diagram early.

[11:27] Ava: will include DPA + dataflow.

[11:30] Benji: couple of quick nitty-gritty: PCI? no; PHI? occasional PII, not PHI. so encryption and KMS is critical.

[11:39] Noah: noted. for KMS we support customer-managed CMKs and HSM-backed keys for Dedicated and Private.

[11:45] Priya: one more question — if we go Dedicated and then want to scale beyond reserved nodes how quickly can Redwood increase capacity? is it days or weeks?

[11:55] Ava: depends on region and demand; in many cases burst capacity can be added within hours, but long-term reserved capacity provisioning for sustained growth may take weeks to match capacity commitments. we'll be transparent about lead times.

[12:09] Maya: ok great. let's talk about pilot content — what figures do you need from us?

[12:15] Ava: 1) 7-day QPS and seq-length histograms 2) list of routes you want in pilot 3) priority for RealTimeQA tenant isolation 4) compliance checklist entries 5) billing contact and procurement timeline.

[12:30] Luis: we'll provide those.

[12:33] Priya: timeline wise we'll aim to supply data by next Friday.

[12:36] Ava: perfect. last part — recap and next steps: we'll send sizing + pricing + security pack by Friday (2027-06-04), schedule the bench kickoff week of 2027-06-14, and Noah will own bench run.

[12:50] Maya: thanks everyone, that was useful.

[12:53] Ava: thanks, we'll follow up with the docs.

[13:00] End recording.

Notes: occasional speaker label drift and audio dropout for Benji around 00:30-02:00. Transcript contains filler words and some mis-transcribed technical names (e.g., model names approximated).
